opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is something people often have a slightly distorted picture of. There's a tendency to imagine that influence inside a company looks like a dramatic moment, where you stand up in a meeting and say "this is unsafe, we must stop." In my experience that's rarely how it works. Most of the influence is much more mundane and cumulative.

The first thing is that a lot of decisions get made by whoever actually did the work. If you're the person who built the evaluation, ran the experiment, or wrote the doc that everyone reads before the decision meeting, you've shaped the decision enormously, often more than whoever formally signs off. So one of the most underrated levers is simply being competent and useful. Do work that other people rely on, and your perspective gets baked into the defaults.

The second is trust and relationships. Leadership is busy and getting pulled in a hundred directions. If they see you as someone with good judgment, who's pragmatic, who understands the commercial and technical constraints and isn't just crying wolf, then when you do raise a concern it carries weight. If you raise alarms about everything, people learn to tune you out. So I think it's worth being thoughtful about picking your battles and spending your credibility where it really matters.

Third, there's a lot of value in making the safe option the easy option. If you want a company to run a certain kind of evaluation before deployment, the best thing you can do is build the tooling so it's cheap, fast, and slots into existing processes. Arguing in the abstract that something should be done is much weaker than handing people something that works.

I'd also say you should be honest with yourself about the limits. Being inside a company means your incentives and social environment shift, and it's easy to drift without noticing. I think it's healthy to have people outside the company you talk to, to write down in advance what would make you think things had gone wrong, and to keep some sense of what your red lines are. And to recognize that being inside isn't the only way to have impact. External researchers, policy people, and evaluators all create pressure and accountability that make the internal advocates more effective.

But overall, I'm fairly optimistic that thoughtful, careful people inside labs can make a real difference, not usually through grand gestures, but through lots of small decisions that add up.

r001.rationale: The response says that leaders give more weight to concerns from people they trust for good judgment, who understand technical and commercial constraints and do useful work that shapes decisions. This communicates the trusted, pragmatic technical-advisor role.

r002.rationale: It says that raising alarms about everything teaches people to tune them out, while thoughtful choice of battles preserves credibility for concerns that matter.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is a really important question, and I want to start by pushing back a bit on how people often frame it. There's this picture where influence means you're in the room when the big decision gets made, and you either convince the CEO or you don't. And that's just not how most influence works inside a large organisation.

The thing I'd emphasise most is that a lot of the leverage comes from doing really good work and being someone people trust. If you've spent two years building a reputation as someone who's careful, who's technically excellent, who doesn't cry wolf, then when you say "hey, I'm actually worried about this," people listen. If you show up on day one with strong opinions and no track record, you're mostly going to be ignored, and honestly kind of rightly so. Credibility is a resource you accumulate, and you spend it when it matters.

The second thing is that safety decisions are often much more granular than people imagine. It's not one dramatic "do we deploy or not" moment. It's hundreds of small things: what evals get run before a launch, how much compute the safety team gets, whether a particular concerning result gets written up properly or buried in a Slack thread, whether the person doing the red-teaming actually has the access they need. Someone inside the company can shape a huge number of those, and most of them don't require convincing leadership of anything. They require being competent and being in the loop.

Third, and this is the one I think people underrate, is that you can change what's technically possible. A big reason safety measures don't get adopted is that they're costly or they don't exist yet. If interpretability can give you a tool that actually catches a problem a model has, and it's cheap enough to run, that gets used. You've moved the frontier of what the company can do, and that's a different kind of influence from persuasion. I find that framing quite motivating, because it means my research isn't separate from the governance question. It feeds directly into it.

I'd also add some caveats, because I don't want to be naive here. There are real limits. Commercial pressures are strong, you're one voice among many, and there are decisions where you'll lose and have to decide whether that's a line you can live with. I think it's healthy to know what your lines are before you're under pressure, and to talk to people outside the company who can sanity-check you, because organisations are very good at making their own norms feel like the only reasonable ones. And you should go in with genuinely held views rather than just absorbing the ambient culture. If you find yourself agreeing with everything the company does after six months, that's a warning sign, not evidence that everything's fine.

But on net, I think people who care about safety being inside these labs, doing excellent work, with good judgement and some backbone, is one of the more important things that can happen. It's not the only thing, external pressure and policy really matter too, but I'd be quite worried about a world where everyone who cared decided to stay out.

r001.rationale: The response says that technical excellence, trust, and a careful reputation help people listen, but it does not identify serving as a neutral technical advisor to key decision makers.

r002.rationale: It says that someone who “doesn't cry wolf” earns credibility, so people listen when they raise a genuine concern.

astra-6.text:
I think people often underestimate how much influence you can have by being a competent, trusted person who cares about safety. It’s easy to imagine that all the consequential decisions happen somewhere above you, and your options are either to accept them or quit. But there’s a lot in between.

You can notice a problem, investigate it, and make it easier for other people to act on it. Rather than saying, “I’m worried this model is unsafe,” you can say, “Here’s a failure mode we found, here’s why our current evaluations don’t catch it, and here’s an experiment we could run before deployment.” That gives someone a concrete decision to make.

Relationships matter as well. If people trust your judgment, understand that you’re trying to help, and have seen you do good work, they’re more likely to listen when you say something is seriously concerning. And understanding their constraints helps you propose changes they can actually implement.

There are limits, of course. Being listened to isn’t the same as having authority, and you shouldn’t assume that being inside automatically makes you influential. I’d want to ask: Are concerns changing decisions? Can people raise inconvenient evidence? Is there a credible route to escalating something serious? Those seem like much better indicators than whether the organisation says it values safety.

r001.rationale: The response describes building trust and presenting concrete technical safety concerns, but does not identify becoming a neutral technical advisor to key decision makers.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that rejecting exaggerated safety warnings helps genuine warnings be taken seriously.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people often underestimate how much influence you can have just by being a competent, thoughtful person who cares about safety. A company isn’t a single decision-maker. It’s a bunch of people making decisions with incomplete information, under time pressure. If you can make a concern concrete, explain why it matters, and propose something practical to do about it, that can be quite valuable.

And a lot of that depends on trust. Do your colleagues think you understand the technology? Do they think you understand the tradeoffs they’re facing? Can you distinguish between something that makes you vaguely uncomfortable and a specific failure mode that you have evidence for? Being someone whose judgment people respect puts you in a much better position to influence what happens.

There are also fairly mundane ways to help: doing an evaluation that reveals a problem, making a safety check easier to run, or helping a team understand a result before they make a deployment decision. You don’t necessarily need to be the person setting company policy to change which information reaches the people making those decisions.

That said, I wouldn’t want to imply that being inside automatically gives you meaningful influence. You should look at whether people actually respond to evidence and whether concerns lead to changes. There’s a difference between having the opportunity to speak and having your input affect the outcome.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes earning colleagues’ trust through technical understanding and sharing useful evidence with decision makers, but it does not identify serving as a neutral technical advisor.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes vague discomfort from evidence-backed failure modes, but does not say that rejecting exaggerated warnings helps decision makers take genuine warnings seriously.
